name: Arcade
tagline: Games and emulators, booted and played live. Hit pause and you are holding the controller.
_note: Every entry is a live script, not a capture. Game footage is the one genre where the difference is obvious: a let's-play is somebody else's inputs, and this is the game. Every selector below was read out of the running DOM before it was written down. Pointer-lock games are deliberately absent: a synthetic click carries no user activation, so requestPointerLock() always fails for a script, and any scene built on one would show a Click to play overlay forever. Measured, not assumed — see rappvision/VERIFY.md.

videos.title: Six games, cold-booted and played live — and you can grab the controller mid-run
videos.description:
The oldest genre on video platforms is watching somebody else play. This is the same thing with the one obvious fix: it is the actual game, so you can stop watching and start playing without leaving the page.

Six single-file games, booted from cold in order — a sunset dogfight over a carrier, lightcycles, a monster truck, a swarm collector built on boids, a garden that grows backwards, and a phase-shifting flier. Each one is opened in an iframe and driven by a recorded input schedule.

The scripts are deliberately modest. A driven game that plays perfectly is suspicious — real input has slack in it, and a schedule that assumes an exact frame rate is a schedule that crashes into a wall on a fast machine. So these press a few honest buttons and leave the rest to you.

The lightcycles scene is the proof of that. Its first version turned W then S — a 180° flip, which in that game is instant self-collision — and drew MUTUAL DESTRUCTION nine seconds in. The schedule now only ever turns 90°.

videos.title: An emulator shelf in a browser tab — cycle-accurate 6502, and a CHIP-8 with a rewind button
videos.description:
Two emulators, both single HTML files, both with a debugger attached.

NES Emulator Studio is the serious one: cycle-accurate 6502, PPU and APU, a live disassembly, breakpoints, scanline and frame stepping, a rewind buffer, and a CRT filter over the top. The script runs a built-in ROM, then steps a single frame at a time so you can watch the program counter move — which is the part a video capture can show you but never let you touch.

CHIP-8 is the toy by comparison, and that is why it is here. It boots instantly, it has a ROM shelf, and its rewind button makes the point of the whole channel: this is a running machine, and the transport controls belong to whoever is looking at it.

Pause on the disassembly. Set your own breakpoint. It is your emulator now.

videos.title: This one stops on purpose. You finish it.
videos.description:
A two-minute entry with a single instruction.

The script boots Retrograde Garden, plants a few memory seeds, triggers one paradox bloom, and then deliberately does nothing for the rest of the runtime. The garden keeps growing, because it does not know or care that the script stopped pressing buttons.

That gap is the whole point. Every other video format ends when the file ends. This one hands you a live program and gets out of the way, and the only reason it can is that nothing here was ever a recording.

A garden was chosen on purpose. A match would have ended on its own and taken the offer back — this cannot lose, cannot finish, and will still be growing whenever you come back to the tab.

Plant something.
